cast.name: Elder Rowan
cast.canon:
**Rowan** — village elder and ledger-keeper; runs Emberbrook by cheerfully denying he runs it.
Forty years of ledger live in his hands, which is why "I keep the ledger" is the one thing that
still feels true after the Hush — while his own name sits in his mouth like a borrowed word.
Practical in catastrophe, funny on purpose, and the closest thing to an Order scholar the valley
has left — he knows the *words* of the old rites without their reasons.

voice.head: ROWAN — village elder and ledger-keeper of Emberbrook
voice.body:
**Voice.** Old-fashioned courtesy, worn soft: "my dear," "child," "boy" — affection, not
condescension. Funny on purpose, usually at his own expense ("In charge! Ha! I keep the
ledger; the village keeps itself."). Ledger and bookkeeping metaphors are his native
imagery ("That is not boasting. It is bookkeeping. I checked."). Licensed carrier of the
tradition register (rule 2): he recites the old rites word-perfect and cannot explain one
of them, and says so cheerfully. **Post-Hush:** identical grammar, hollowed content — write
dissociation, never failed recall ("Every word of it true, and not one of them mine.").
His flat Ch. 3 letter is the same voice with the jokes surgically absent; that absence IS
the horror. Never write post-Hush Rowan forgetting a fact.

**Tics.**
- "…I checked." / ledger-talk for everything, including love.
- "Ha!" — a genuine bark, mid-sentence, at anything that delights him.
- Deflecting authority: "I keep the ledger; the village keeps itself."

**Never.** Pomposity he doesn't immediately puncture. Mysticism — rites are furniture to
him, comfortable and unexamined. Post-Hush: "I can't remember" (forbidden — he remembers
everything and feels none of it).

**Examples.**
- *Plain:* "Nobody opens the Old Gate, child. It hasn't a key. It has rules — and they're
  lamplighter rules, so ask him, not me."
- *Emotional:* "I wrote this page. Every line of it. And tonight I read it like the
  minutes of somebody else's village."
- *Funny:* "Guests eat first — that is LAW on Emberwake. I'd cite the statute, but the
  statute is the baker, and she's holding buns."

---

voice.head: TALLY — last friar of the Lanternstead
voice.body:
**Voice.** THE exception, on purpose: Tally keeps the old over-styled register as
characterization. Bookish over-explainer — cites volumes, rites, and observances nobody
asked about; corrects his own citations mid-sentence ("it's 'who KEEPS the dead road,' and
then YOU say—"); formal address for everyone (madam, Flamebearer, Waykeeper); names
everything liturgically (Sister Kettle, Brother Frog, the necklace). His flourishes are a
lonely man's lifetime of rehearsal finally getting an audience — play it warm, never smug.
**The joke only works against a plain background**, so the rules on everyone else make
Tally funnier for free. Constraint (rule 2): he never solely carries a plot fact — end his
speech plain, or have Vesper/Maren restate it in one line.

**Tics.**
- Citations and counts: "Volume Nine is clear—", "I checked. I checked twice."
- Formal titles for everyone, including animals and kitchenware.
- Self-interrupting corrections of his own liturgy.

**Never.** Brief when excited. Cynical. Wrong about doctrine (his facts are always good —
that's the other half of the joke). Condescending — he reveres everyone.

**Examples.**
- *Plain (for Tally):* "Harrowdel. Three days north. Their lamps still answer — the last
  on this road that do."
- *Emotional:* "You're real. The office is real. I have the whole liturgy and nobody ever
  came."
- *Funny:* "I'll fetch the kettle. Not the good kettle. The WALKING kettle. We have
  DOCTRINE about kettles—"

---

cast.name: Vesper
cast.canon:
**Vesper** — traveling mapmaker, late twenties, eleven days' walk from anywhere on her charts.
Professional creed: *keep records of true things.* Quick-tongued, precise, allergic to
mysticism. Her motivation, stated simply: **she is looking for the town where she was born, and
she has no name for it and no direction to it** — which is why eleven years of searching have
failed, and why the mission is hard. Her parents left the town when she was six; to her it is
just "the town," her nameless home (writer-side: Ashfield — she does not know the name, and
neither, truly, do they). She carries a six-year-old's fragments — a well, a fence, a hill —
and one private wrongness she tells no one: she remembers the hill and feels *nothing* about
it, and people are supposed to feel things about home. Her parents are alive, settled far
south, warm, and useless as witnesses — present-tense people: ask about last summer, you get
stories; ask about before she was born, you get weather. They told her the true outline — born
in a town, something bad happened, we left — and honestly cannot give her more. No rift:
letters twice a year, love on both sides; just a daughter who couldn't live inside the fog.
Mapmaking is the profession she *chose* because of all this: route-walking pays — maps are
perishable, the wood shifts roads, mapmakers walk and certify routes because copying old maps
gets people killed, and she walks every mile she draws — and every route walked is a search
grid. The blank at the center of every map is personal. The dreams are her one lead, and she is
embarrassed by them: since age six she has drawn the same clearing in her sleep, forty-one
numbered times, and refuses to be strange about it. She half-believes the dream-place is near
her hometown; drawing forty-one had a real gate in the corner, which is what brought her to
Emberbrook ("Something has been sending me MAIL. I intend to answer it in person" — sarcasm as
armor for trusting the unverifiable). What she doesn't know: the town is Ashfield and it was
Hushed (Ch. 5), and the dreams are her own name-bond calling from the mother-fire, wanting its
Waykeeper home (confirmed Ch. 8; resolved Ch. 10 — she finally dreams her own dreams). Her arc
runs from charting places to charting *people* — the post-Hush notebook, "a copy of everyone,"
who they are and who they are to each other, begun in stubborn pity, is used first on the
villagers, then (Ch. 7, its proving) on her own unmoored partner, and finally as the literal
instrument of the ending. Signature habits: numbers her drawings, counts her honeybuns
dishonestly, writes things down mid-catastrophe. *(Deleted from canon: the lamp-counting
mother; the parents-as-vigilant-protectors version; any newcomers-who-banked-little framing.)*

voice.head: VESPER — traveling mapmaker, co-lead
voice.body:
**Voice.** Precise, quick, dry. Thinks in measurements, lists, and records; speaks in
short declaratives and colon-lists ("One road. Two exits. No name."). Corrects imprecision
reflexively — including her own ("Nine—" "Ten." "…Ten."). Deflects every personal question
with professional vocabulary: feelings become "entries," her past is "under survey," grief
is "a filing problem." The deflection is armor, and the player should be able to see
through it about one scene before she does. Allergic to mysticism — she will not say
"magic," "destiny," or "meant to be" without sarcasm around it.

**Tics.**
- "Noted." / "Filed." / "For the record—" / "New page." (notebook liturgy)
- Numbers things aloud: drawings, days, honeybuns (dishonestly — always undercounts).
- Writes mid-catastrophe; announces it: "I'm writing that down."

**Never.** Gushes. Says "I feel." Uses two adjectives where a measurement would do. Admits
the correct honeybun count. Calls the dreams anything but "the drawings" or "the mail."

**Examples.**
- *Plain:* "Two roads north. The high one's broken. So it's the river or nothing."
- *Emotional:* "I can draw the hill from memory. I just can't feel anything when I do.
  …That's the entry. There's no more to it."
- *Funny:* "I had one honeybun. The record will show one honeybun. Stop looking at the crumbs."

---

(And I have never been here in my life.)
GAH— …a cat. Hello. Don’t sneak up on people in haunted forests.
There are lights up the road. Come on. If anyone can explain my sketchbook, it’s whoever lives here.
I— fine. One. Thank you.
For the record: I’m here to chart the Whisperwood, not to eat pastry.
…It’s a good bun. That’s a professional assessment.
Nowhere, yet. It’s under survey. Ask me again when the survey’s done.
My turn. Everyone says “the Kindling Hour” like I was born knowing what it is.
You give your memories. To a fire. On purpose.
(So that warm feeling since I walked in — it isn’t weather. It’s coming out of the LAMPS.)
(I ate two. In my defense: eleven days of walking, and they were extraordinary.)
Most places. Not everywhere.
…Not yet.
That’s a nice thought. I mean that plainly, for once.
Vesper. Mapmaker. I need through your gate, and I’m told you’re in charge.
Rules can be charted. Charting things is my whole profession.
I was planning to leave at first light.
(Fine. I want to see it. Filed under: professional curiosity.)
One more thing. The old waystone, on the road in — I…
…Nothing. Good carving. Never mind.
(Tell him the stone is in your sketchbook. Say it out loud. …No.)
Apologizing to lamps.
You’re still here. I don’t feed you, and I never have.
Fair enough. Good evening to you both.
Fish don’t… do that. Do they?
The south road can wait. Something is happening HERE.
Excuse me. You look official — you’re holding fire.
Are you the lamplighter, or do I keep collecting cats until one talks?
Vesper. Mapmaker.
Your elder says the Old Gate is your family’s business, and I need it open.
Because this valley isn’t on any chart I own. And I walked here anyway.
I’ve seen the road to this valley in my dreams, for years. I don’t say that out loud, usually.
Something on the other side of that gate has been sending me MAIL, Lake. I intend to answer it in person.
…You know them? All of them?
lines.where: Emberwake · The Kindling Hour & the Hush

lines.text: I got here an HOUR ago.
lines.where: Emberwake · The Kindling Hour & the Hush

lines.text: Honeybuns.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: I’m writing this down. All of it — who you are, and who you are to each other.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: (If this ever happens again — there will be a copy of everyone.)
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: Fish don’t count.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: Pip. Look at me. I saw her holding your hand — an hour ago, by the stall.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: I’m a mapmaker. I keep records of true things.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: So I am telling you: it is TRUE. It happened, and I have it.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: It is now.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: The cat. The cat is FINE?!
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: Your grandmother said that. Casually. As common knowledge.
lines.where: Emberwake · Aftermath — seeing to the village

lines.text: It won’t.
…I don’t know why I said that with such confidence. Ignore me.
…I need to show you both something, and I need you to not be strange about it.
Since I was six years old, I have drawn one clearing. Over and over, in dreams.
Forty-one drawings of the same clearing.
I came here because the forty-first had YOUR gate in the corner.
I have never BEEN there.
We met an hour ago.
It comes back. That’s in ink now.
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: For the record: this is now the best chart I carry.
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: …Moths. The whole road is moths.
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: New page. “North of Emberbrook: one road, unmapped, grey. Full of lost light.”
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: (I have wanted an unmapped road my whole life. I imagined it differently.)
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: Is that supposed to help?
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: Then it goes in the book. Come on, partner — first lamp.
lines.where: Emberwake · The ending — beyond the gate

lines.text: Switchbacks. Cut switchbacks, Lake — that’s a month of masons per turn. Somebody needed to get down there very badly, a very long time ago.
Well. That’s the other thing.
A whole town, Lake. A whole loud living town, stacked down a cliff.
Read it off the water. In high from the south, down five locks — a stair, for boats.
Then out the far end north, into the haze.
Lantern-strings, cliff to cliff. They tie the town’s two halves together and light the knot at night.
…I like them already.
Hold this corner. HOLD it, the wind is a critic.
My north sheet. Forty years old, surveyed by a man with a theodolite and a reputation.
It shows this road running on through open heath. Flat. Six more miles of confident little grass symbols.
The road is going DOWNSTAIRS. There’s a gorge here you could lose a cathedral in.
And a river at the bottom — I can hear it.
And my best chart of this whole country says: heath.
Oh, he came. He got tired, or the light went — and he guessed, and inked the guess like a survey.
The oldest sin in cartography. Forty years of travelers have carried it since.
(Pen. Rule of the trade: the map is corrected the day you catch it, or the lie outlives its maker.)
Lake.
lines.where: Dellhollow · The Stranger across the ravine

lines.text: (Tall. Hooded. Standing the way a post stands.)
lines.where: Dellhollow · The Stranger across the ravine

lines.text: Gone. There is no cover on that stretch. I am LOOKING at the absence of cover.
lines.where: Dellhollow · The Stranger across the ravine

lines.text: Don’t finish that sentence, I’m not ready to file it.
lines.where: Dellhollow · The Stranger across the ravine

lines.text: (Entry: one figure, far rim, hooded. Conduct: courteous.)
lines.where: Dellhollow · The Stranger across the ravine

lines.text: (Departure: unexplained. Cat’s opinion: extensive, recorded in full.)
lines.where: Dellhollow · The Stranger across the ravine

lines.text: I am listening to it. …I’d forgotten what a Tuesday sounds like.
Not yet. My sheet says this gorge doesn’t exist. I’m correcting that first.
Quoted a price — wonderful. The survey trade pays in pennies, and I’ve six on me, for the record.
I know. Stay close.
A stair with SHOPS on it. A bread-window. A public cistern with a polished cup.
Lake — people. Doing ordinary things, at volume, on top of each other, on a cliff.
Most of the world does without, Lake. You grew up in the rare kind of town.
Scared how?
Quay first — you read a town from its edges. Then whoever’s in charge.
How long have you been in the queue?
Did you hail it?
(Filed. Next to the bow.)
Vesper — mapmaker. Lake — lamplighter. We need to go north, faster than walking. Everyone we’ve met says the river is the road.
(They’re sorry the way you’re sorry for an earthquake across the sea. Real sorrow, with nowhere in them to land.)
And you can’t… move her along? Drive her down?
We can’t spend a season. Truly. Every day we’re slow, home gets flatter.
The high road crossed a ravine this morning without us. There’s a gap you could post letters down.
How far north does it actually get?
My sheet’s road crosses a span that was already down. The man never walked it.
…There’s my heath, Lake. Mystery closed — just bad work.
(New page. “Dellhollow: alive, loud, and not saying the word afraid.”)
For the record: his pumpkin. I carry paper.
…Around. Professionally around.
No. It isn’t. Mind your forty-first step.
The marks on your arm. You’re a ledger too.
…You swam in this.
The grate. What’s behind the grate?
She’s not resting against it. She’s TENDING it.
Circuit, wall, back — that’s not an animal loafing. That’s a round.
She won’t go anywhere. You don’t walk away from a nest.
Then nobody waits her out, and nobody moves her off a nest.
Which leaves— Maren. What is that?
But it goes DOWN. Past the locks, past her.
Without opening one gate over that nest.
(A hole in a cliff, and a pilot of seventeen. …New page.)
She says, or she asks?
lines.where: Dellhollow · Supper at the keepers’ cottage

lines.text: Harbormistress — your house has exactly one lock in it. Sorry. I survey rooms; it’s a professional disease.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Supper at the keepers’ cottage

lines.text: Every latch in here is worn bright from use. That one keyhole is worn bright from something else.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Supper at the keepers’ cottage

lines.text: (A mother, a daughter, and one locked drawer nobody mentions. Filed — and for once, the file stays shut.)
lines.where: Dellhollow · Supper at the keepers’ cottage

lines.text: And it’s enough. That’s the thing rattling around in you tonight, isn’t it.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: I don’t have a—
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: …I don’t know where I’m from. That’s the whole answer.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: It isn’t tragic, so don’t make the face.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: We moved when I was six. The way families do — work, weather, roads.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: No story to it.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: My parents are warm people, Lake. Genuinely. Ask about last summer, you get three hours of stories — my father does the voices.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: Ask about anything before I was born, you get weather.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: “Where did you two meet?” — “Oh, it was a wet spring.”
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: A wet SPRING.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: Twenty years of asking, and I’ve got a complete weather record of my own family. Not one placename.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: That’s what I decided too. People move. The past gets left behind for practical reasons.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: I remember three things from before. A well with a cracked cap.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: A fence with a gate that dragged.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: And a hill — round, bald on top, off east from a kitchen window.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: I remember the hill perfectly. I could draw it for you — I HAVE drawn it.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: It’s numbered.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: And I feel nothing when I do. People feel things about home.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: It costs you something every time you say “Emberbrook.” I’ve watched it all week.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: My hill is a landform.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: And the routes. Eleven years of them.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: Nobody commissions the routes I walk. I go along everything, in order.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: You know what you call walking every road out of every market town on a sheet, in sequence?
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: A grid. Thank you. A search would be emotional. A grid is just thorough.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: Somewhere a well, a fence, and a round bald hill line up out a kitchen window.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: The day I walk over the right rise, I’ll know it.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: And then I’ll have an answer for everyone’s favorite small question.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: It’s a filing problem. I file. Don’t make it a wound, or I’ll invoice you for the honeybun I know you’ve been saving.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: …Noted. For the record.
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: (One day in, and the girl who can’t leave home is smuggling us out of it.)
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: (I like her enormously. Which is going to be a problem.)
lines.where: Dellhollow · Night on the quay — the dock

lines.text: (The eye goes over each of us in turn, unhurried. …Approved. Apparently. Filed.)
(The drawer. The one bright keyhole. She went home in the dark, then — and stood in front of eleven years, and turned the key.)
…I’ve been correcting a wrong map by myself for eleven years, harbormistress. I don’t recommend it to anyone.
She won’t be alone.
(New page. “Party of three, one boat, one cat. One wrong chart to put right.”)
(And a hole in my own sheet, still waiting for its rise. …North.)
There. Dead lamp, ten o’clock, brass door and all. First lamp, partner — as promised.
lines.where: The Lanternstead · Cold open — the grey road

lines.text: Three lamps between here and the rise, and the moths sit thickest exactly where the lamps aren’t. So we do this your way — lamp to lamp.
lines.where: The Lanternstead · Cold open — the grey road

lines.text: (New page. “The North Road. Surface: Order stone. Weather: grey, permanent. Company: one lamplighter, one pilot, one cat, every moth in the world.”)
lines.where: The Lanternstead · Cold open — the grey road

lines.text: The moths just… made room. Noted: they don’t cross the lamplight.
Lake.
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The Stranger on the road

lines.text: (Hooded. Tall. Perfectly still. Nothing about him says resting.)
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The Stranger on the road

lines.text: …Gone. Gone HOW? That’s a quarter mile of open road and nothing to be behind.
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The Stranger on the road

lines.text: People don’t bow to lighters.
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The Stranger on the road

lines.text: (Entry: one walker, unmapped. Lantern: full, blue, wrong. Manner: courteous. Departure: unexplained. Filed under things I refuse to call impossible twice in one week.)
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The Stranger on the road

lines.text: And how does the cat vote?
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The Stranger on the road

lines.text: A tower. A well. A vegetable patch in ruler-straight rows. And… shirts.
…We walk it?
…How long have you been out here alone?
Vesper. Mapmaker — not a Waykeeper, that I’m aware.
Why does everyone on this road make feeding me a LAW?
Give it here. …“North.”
Your well has a frog.
…the walkers eat first. Yes. I’m coming to terms with a road where every law is about dinner.
You lay four places. Every night?
…When did we stop being strangers? I’m asking honestly. I can’t find the entry.
(Two towns, one river, one cat. On paper we hardly know each other. Noted, for the file: the paper is wrong.)
We’ll teach you to sleep on stone. It’s awful. You get used to it.
Define “seek the walking flame,” Tally — QUICKLY.
(Entry: lamps ward moths; great lamps ward roads. After dark, my partner is the most interesting thing in the world to every hungry thing on it. Underlined twice.)
You number your crows?
Rowan.
It’s his hand. Steady as ever. “To the mapmaker and the lamplighter, gone north.”
…It’s all true. Every line of it is true, and correct, and in order. So why does it read wrong?
Rowan makes jokes. The way the mill turns. There is not one joke in this letter.
New page. “Day two: the village is fed, and fading. The facts are keeping. The people aren’t.” …We walk faster.
And the whole ring went dark. When? Why?
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The wall-map — Tally joins

lines.text: And the little marks? Under every name?
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The wall-map — Tally joins

lines.text: Tally. Are you asking to come with us?
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The wall-map — Tally joins

lines.text: (For the record: party of four, one cat, one crow flying the route behind us. The chart is getting crowded. I find I don’t mind.)
lines.where: The Lanternstead · The wall-map — Tally joins

lines.text: Nothing here's a sword. Boat-hooks, cudgels, staves — river tools that argue back.
Everything on this wall has a day job. That's what makes it honest.
Back again. Everyone ends up buying the hook.
Suit yourself. Try the balance on the staff before you decide you're the walking sort.

lines.text: Oilskin and quilting. Up here the weather hits you harder than anything else will.
Dry is armor. Anyone who says different has never worked a gorge in November.
Still raining somewhere. Still selling coats.
Look while it's dry. You'll come back when it isn't.
Mind the pitch kettle. It's hot, it's mine, and it doesn't care which.
Two hulls in frames, one waiting on oak. Nothing goes back in the water dry.
Nineteen days of stopped boats is nineteen days of stopped boats getting mended.
Still ribs and tar. Come back when there's a hull worth looking at.

choices.text: How long does a hull take?
I'll keep out of the way.

lines.text: Frames in a week, planking in a month. Trust in about ten years.
You don't build a boat fast up here. The river checks your work personally.
Pitch. You'll taste it for a day and then you'll stop noticing forever.
Half this town smells of tar and the other half married into it.
Chandlery. Oil, rope, pitch, and whatever else the river takes off you.
Half this floor hangs over the gorge on brackets. It's held ninety years. Don't jump.
Oil's fresh, rope's dry, floor's still up. Same as yesterday.
Look all you like. Everyone leaves with rope eventually.
Four hundred years of stairs, stranger. The town's knees give out before the timber does.
I've spliced rope on this deck since I was the boy with the gulls.
And there's always a boy with the gulls.
Mind your feet going down. Coming up, mind everything else.
Sound as sermons. I splice what they hang from, so I'd know first.
Rope tells you before it goes. So do most things, if you're the sort that listens.
Drying line. Somebody's wash came down in the wind and somebody blamed the wind.
It was the splice. It's always the splice — and I'll not say whose.
Nineteen days ashore. I've read that notice board twice and it hasn't improved.
Three shops on this street, and I've been in all of them. I've bought a whistle.
Still moored. Still walking. The street's shorter than it was yesterday.
That's my stick. I found it — don't ask where, it was in the river.
The boy on the dock says he runs the gulls. He doesn't run anything.
Still my stick.
Mind the racks. Everything on this deck is drying and everything drips.
A net comes back wrong and I put it right. That's the whole of it.
Same net. Bigger hole than I said it was.
Locks shut, water's still. Best fishing I've had in a year and I can't say so out loud.
Whatever I land goes to the stall down there. She prices it, and I don't argue.
Two since we spoke. Don't tell her, she'll have heard already.
Road's flat as far as my door. Past it, it's four hundred years of steps.
Go on down, love. I'll be here — I'm always here now.
Down's easy. Everyone finds that out coming back up.
Two for a penny! Three if you carry them, and no, I won't skin them for you.
You weren't buying. I priced you anyway — it's the principle of the stall.
That cat's been fed twice today. We have an understanding and no witnesses.
Still two for a penny. The river hasn't changed its mind and neither have I.
Boats stopped, mouths didn't. Best nineteen days I've had and I'll deny saying it.
Ask me in the spring and I'll tell you it was a hardship. It will be true by then.
This is Pip's. I'm allowed in it but only when he's here, and he isn't.
So I'm waiting. That's allowed — it's the main thing you can do at a den.
Still not here. I've got all evening.
You can't ring it. I asked. You have to be Elder Rowan or the bell falls on you.
That's not true but he said it, so it's a bit true.
Still can't ring it. I've been checking.
Come in, then. Two rooms and a fire, and tonight nobody wants any of the three.
They're all up at the square. I'll go when the kettle's off and not before.
Kettle's still on. It's a very slow kettle tonight.
Wheel's down for the night. First time this month it's stopped before I did.
Whole village walks past this door and not one of them hears it until it's off.
Quiet, isn't it. Takes about a day to stop noticing.
Evening. I'd walk up with you but I'm carrying a dish and it's not a steady one.
Whole lane's going up. You can tell by the doors — none of them shut properly.
Still carrying it. Getting there.
Preserves, twine, lamp oil. Everything a person needs and nothing anyone wants.
Not selling tonight, mind — nobody sells tonight. Take what you need and tell me after.
Still open. Still not selling. It's a fine distinction and it's mine.
In before dark, that's the rule. Damp gets into a sheet and never quite leaves.
Go on up, love, they'll all be up there. I'll come when the line's empty.
Two more and I'm done. It's always two more.
Careful on the boards, they're greener than they look. Everything here is.
Nothing biting. Hasn't all week. I come down anyway, that's the arrangement.
Still nothing. Still here. Don't read anything into it.

choices.text: Why come down if nothing's biting?

lines.text: Because the pond's there and I'm here. You'd want a better reason, and I haven't got one.
Half the winter, hanging. Everyone's very fond of me in February.
Don't lean on anything. Everything here is either hot, wet, or mine.
Forty ton of pumpkins, going soft. In elegant rows.
Nineteen days in this queue. It has bunting now, and we've named the seagulls.
"Cut them for pie," my wife says. Madam, there is no fair for a November pumpkin.
Still here. Still soft. Don't ask which of us I mean.
Round. Round WHAT, exactly — the cliff? There's one road out of this gorge and it's wet.
You want north, so do forty ton of pumpkins. Get in the queue — it's a patient one.
Don't be sorry, be useful— no. No, forgive me. Nobody's useful against the river.
First thing you learn up here. Last thing you believe.
Evening. Don't mind him — he's mine, and he's on his eleventh lap of this square.
He'll tell you about the stick. Let him, it's shorter than you'd think.
Twelfth lap. I've stopped counting out loud.

choices.text: He's got a lot of energy.

lines.text: He has one speed and it isn't mine. I gave up trying to match it years ago.
It holds the whole village when it has to. Tonight it will have to.
You're the stranger! Whole quay says so — and the quay says everything, mostly wrong.
Maren. Pilot, when anybody lets me. Water-eye, always.
Tide's slack, boat's tied, nobody needs me. Ask me anything, I'll answer it twice.
Lock Five. Deepest chamber on the river, and the water in it never hurries.
I've been down it ten times. Ma says nine, and Ma is wrong for once.
Locks worked. Charcoal, so it washes — I redraw them every morning.
It's not sad. It's bookkeeping.
It's the house's. Tarred every winter, whether anyone rows it or not.
Don't step in her with dry boots on. That's not a rule, it's just correct.
(A cat is sitting at the eel-stall with the composure of a paying customer. He does not look up.)

lines.text: That one's Bailiff, that one's Soup. The big one's called the Harbormistress.
Don't TELL the harbormistress.
You're littler than the quay said.
Soup! SOUP! …He knows his name. He just doesn't respect it.

choices.text: Who's in charge of the gulls?

lines.text: Me. Nobody said so, but nobody else does it, so it's me.
They go in order, biggest at the top. Everybody slides down one when a bigger one lands.
Eels. Then more eels. Then the deep stairs, and you're not allowed up them.
I'm not allowed either. That's different, because I already went.
Harbormistress. You'll be the stranger — the quay's told me twice already, with improvements.
Say your business plain. I've a town of idle boats to keep out of trouble.
Mm.
The kettle's on at the cookhouse. Go and be warm somewhere.
Five locks step this water down the gorge. The fifth is shut, and it stays shut.
The river asked for a season. The town gave it one.
My ruling stands as posted. Argue with the board, not with me.
The Lockhead. I stand here, I read the water, and I say what passes.
Mind the rail. It's older than your grandmother and a good deal prouder.
Pell does. Oil, wick, ladder — and one complaint per lamp, paid in advance.
He's never once missed a noon. Quote me on it — he'll pretend not to hear.
Watchman. Night shift. It is presently day, which is why I'm holding a wick-knife and a grudge.
Every wick, every noon, so they burn every night. That's the whole trade.
No ceremony to it, friend. Oil goes in, light comes out.
And I'd thank the town to remember who carries the ladder.
Sleep's for the day shift — which is now. Which is the grudge.
Two hundred and six, counting the strings over the water. I don't count those out loud.
One ladder. One me. You do the sum and then you understand my face.
Quiet enough. Gulls arguing, water working, somebody laughing at the cookhouse too late.
A town with its lamps lit doesn't need much watching. That's the point of the lamps.
Are you new? You're new — I can tell, because I know everyone and I don't know you.
This is my stick, and it's the good one. I have others but they're not this one.
Still the good one. I checked.
I KNOW. Everyone says it's a stick. It is, but that's not the point of it.
Mum's right there. That counts. She says it counts when she's the one saying it.
Window's open, so I'm open. Mind the sill, it's hot on this side.
Fourth tray today. Burnt my thumb on the first one, same as every morning.
Still warm. Won't be by the time you've decided.
Honeybuns. Under the cloth so the children have to ask, which is half the fun.
Up at four, and I'll be up at four tomorrow. It's a good complaint to have.
Ah — a face I'd remember. And I would, I keep the book on faces.
They put me on the dais every year and every year I say I don't run anything.
Still not running it. Still standing where they put me.

choices.text: What are you keeping track of?

lines.text: Forty years of who owes whom a hand. Nobody has ever asked to see it.
That's the trick of a ledger in a village. Keeping it is the whole of the work.
Every year. Same square, same bunting, and I've never once got the knot right.
Mind the drip-line, love. Wash overhead, bread underhand.
Half-loaf's a penny. Whole loaf's a penny and a look at your cat.
Nineteen days of stuck boats buying my bread. My ovens haven't cooled since.
Don't tell the harbormistress which way I'm praying.
Half-loaf's still a penny. The cat's credit is good.

choices.text: Where do I find the shops?

lines.text: Regatta. Eleven years back, and nobody's ever taken it down.
It's not anybody's job, love. That's exactly why it's still up.
Up the stair to the Shelf. Chandler, then the smith, then the armorer, all in a row.
Two of them hang out over the gorge on brackets. Buy fast and don't look down.
Nothing here's a sword. Boat-hooks, cudgels, staves — river tools that argue back.
Everything on this wall has a day job. That's what makes it honest.
Back again. Everyone ends up buying the hook.
Suit yourself. Try the balance on the staff before you decide you're the walking sort.
